claim: Pancreatic ATP-sensitive K+ channels (KATP) comprise four inward rectifier subunits (Kir6.2), each associated with a sulphonylurea receptor (SUR1).
source: Pancreatic ATP-sensitive K+ channels (KATP) comprise four inward rectifier subunits (Kir6.2), each associated with a sulphonylurea receptor (SUR1).
evidence: This is established knowledge about KATP channel structure, supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: ATP/ADP binding to Kir6.2 shuts KATP.
source: ATP/ADP binding to Kir6.2 shuts KATP.
evidence: This is established knowledge cited in the introduction with references to Tucker et al., 1997 and Proks et al., 2010.

claim: Mg-nucleotide binding to SUR1 stimulates KATP.
source: Mg-nucleotide binding to SUR1 stimulates KATP.
evidence: This is established knowledge cited in the introduction with references to Nichols et al., 1996 and Tucker et al., 1997.

claim: In the absence of Mg2+, SUR1 increases the apparent affinity for nucleotide inhibition at Kir6.2 by an unknown mechanism.
source: In the absence of Mg2+, SUR1 increases the apparent affinity for nucleotide inhibition at Kir6.2 by an unknown mechanism.
evidence: This is cited knowledge from Tucker et al., 1997, and the unknown mechanism is what the study aims to investigate.

claim: Fits to combined data sets suggest that KATP closes with only one nucleotide molecule bound.
source: Fits to combined data sets suggest that KATP closes with only one nucleotide molecule bound.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's data analysis using MWC-type models.

claim: A Kir6.2 mutation (C166S) that increases channel activity did not affect nucleotide binding, but greatly perturbed the ability of bound nucleotide to inhibit KATP.
source: A Kir6.2 mutation (C166S) that increases channel activity did not affect nucleotide binding, but greatly perturbed the ability of bound nucleotide to inhibit KATP.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experimental data on the C166S mutant.

claim: Mutations at position K205 in SUR1 affected both nucleotide affinity and the ability of bound nucleotide to inhibit KATP.
source: Mutations at position K205 in SUR1 affected both nucleotide affinity and the ability of bound nucleotide to inhibit KATP.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experimental data on SUR1-K205 mutants.

claim: SUR1 has a dual role in KATP inhibition, both in directly contributing to nucleotide binding and in stabilising the nucleotide-bound closed state.
source: This suggests a dual role for SUR1 in KATP inhibition, both in directly contributing to nucleotide binding and in stabilising the nucleotide-bound closed state.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data on SUR1-K205 mutants.

claim: In pancreatic β-cells, closure of KATP in response to glucose uptake triggers insulin secretion.
source: In pancreatic β-cells, closure of KATP in response to glucose uptake triggers insulin secretion.
evidence: This is established knowledge about KATP channel function in β-cells.

claim: Mutations in KATP that affect its response to changes in cellular metabolism cause diseases of insulin secretion, for example neonatal diabetes and persistent hyperinsulinemic hypoglycaemia of infancy (PHHI; Quan et al., 2011; Ashcroft et al., 2017).
source: As such, mutations in KATP that affect its response to changes in cellular metabolism cause diseases of insulin secretion, for example neonatal diabetes and persistent hyperinsulinemic hypoglycaemia of infancy (PHHI; Quan et al., 2011; Ashcroft et al., 2017).
evidence: This is cited knowledge about disease-causing mutations in KATP.

claim: KATP is composed of four inwardly rectifying K+ channel subunits (Kir6.2 in pancreatic β-cells), which form the channel pore, and four modulatory sulphonylurea receptor subunits (SUR1 in β-cells; Figure 1A; Aguilar-Bryan et al., 1995; Inagaki et al., 1995; Sakura et al., 1995; Inagaki et al., 1997).
source: KATP is composed of four inwardly rectifying K+ channel subunits (Kir6.2 in pancreatic β-cells), which form the channel pore, and four modulatory sulphonylurea receptor subunits (SUR1 in β-cells; Figure 1A; Aguilar-Bryan et al., 1995; Inagaki et al., 1995; Sakura et al., 1995; Inagaki et al., 1997).
evidence: This is cited knowledge about KATP channel structure, also illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: SUR1 is a member of the ABC transporter family but lacks any transport activity (Aguilar-Bryan et al., 1995; Tusnády et al., 1997).
source: SUR1 is a member of the ABC transporter family but lacks any transport activity (Aguilar-Bryan et al., 1995; Tusnády et al., 1997).
evidence: This is cited knowledge about SUR1's classification and function.

claim: KATP responds to metabolism via adenine nucleotide binding to three distinct classes of intracellular nucleotide-binding site (one on each Kir6.2 subunit and two on each SUR1 subunit—making twelve sites in total [Vedovato et al., 2015]).
source: KATP responds to metabolism via adenine nucleotide binding to three distinct classes of intracellular nucleotide-binding site (one on each Kir6.2 subunit and two on each SUR1 subunit—making twelve sites in total [Vedovato et al., 2015]).
evidence: This is cited knowledge about the nucleotide binding sites on KATP.

claim: Binding of nucleotides to SUR1 stimulates KATP (Nichols et al., 1996; Tucker et al., 1997).
source: whereas binding of nucleotides to SUR1 stimulates KATP (Nichols et al., 1996; Tucker et al., 1997).
evidence: This is cited knowledge about nucleotide stimulation of KATP.

claim: The stimulatory activity of nucleotides on KATP depends on Mg2+ (Gribble et al., 1998).
source: The stimulatory activity of nucleotides on KATP depends on Mg2+ (Gribble et al., 1998)
evidence: This is cited knowledge about the Mg2+ dependence of nucleotide stimulation.

claim: The inhibitory effect of nucleotides on Kir6.2 does not depend on Mg2+ (Tucker et al., 1997).
source: whereas their inhibitory effect on Kir6.2 does not (Tucker et al., 1997).
evidence: This is cited knowledge about the Mg2+ independence of nucleotide inhibition.

claim: SUR1 is responsible for high-affinity inhibition of KATP by antidiabetic sulphonylureas and glinides as well as activation by KATP-specific K+ channel openers (Tucker et al., 1997).
source: SUR1 is also responsible for high-affinity inhibition of KATP by antidiabetic sulphonylureas and glinides as well as activation by KATP-specific K+ channel openers (Tucker et al., 1997).
evidence: This is cited knowledge about SUR1's role in drug sensitivity.

claim: SUR1 and Kir6.2 must co-assemble to ensure mutual exit from the endoplasmic reticulum and correct trafficking to the plasma membrane (Zerangue et al., 1999).
source: Finally, SUR1 and Kir6.2 must co-assemble to ensure mutual exit from the endoplasmic reticulum and correct trafficking to the plasma membrane (Zerangue et al., 1999).
evidence: This is cited knowledge about SUR1 and Kir6.2 trafficking.

claim: ANAP was replaced at position 311 (W311) of Kir6.2, which is 26 Å from the location of the inhibitory nucleotide-binding site.
source: To measure binding to Kir6.2 in the complete KATP complex (four full-length Kir6.2 subunits co-expressed with four full-length SUR1 subunits), we replaced a tryptophan at position 311 (W311) of Kir6.2 that is 26 Å from the location of the inhibitory nucleotide-binding site with ANAP (Figure 1C)
evidence: This is based on structural data and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: 91% FRET efficiency is expected between ANAP at position 311 and a TNP-ATP molecule bound to Kir6.2.
source: Based on the theoretical FRET efficiency calculated from the Förster equation and available cryo-EM structures (Martin et al., 2017; Martin et al., 2019), we expect 91% FRET efficiency between ANAP at position 311 and a TNP-ATP molecule bound to Kir6.2
evidence: This is calculated from the Förster equation using structural data.

claim: Only 4% FRET efficiency is expected between ANAP at position 311 and TNP-ATP bound to the closest nucleotide-binding site on SUR1.
source: and only 4% FRET efficiency to TNP-ATP bound to the closest nucleotide-binding site on SUR1 (nucleotide binding site 1; Figure 1C; Figure 1D).
evidence: This is calculated from the Förster equation using structural data and shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Full length, fully ANAP-labelled Kir6.2 protein was produced and successfully trafficked to the membrane in the presence of SUR1.
source: When cultured in the presence of ANAP, full length, fully ANAP-labelled Kir6.2 protein was produced and successfully trafficked to the membrane in the presence of SUR1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1; see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is demonstrated by western blots and confocal microscopy shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Kir6.2*-GFP + SUR1 exhibited nearly identical sensitivity to ATP inhibition as Kir6.2-GFP + SUR1.
source: Kir6.2*-GFP + SUR1 exhibited nearly identical sensitivity to ATP inhibition as Kir6.2-GFP + SUR1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A)
evidence: This is demonstrated by patch-clamp data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Replacement of W311 with ANAP did not affect inhibition of KATP by ATP.
source: indicating that replacement of W311 with ANAP did not affect inhibition of KATP.
evidence: This is inferred from the similar ATP sensitivity of Kir6.2*-GFP + SUR1 and Kir6.2-GFP + SUR1.

claim: Kir6.2*-GFP was not detected at the plasma membrane in the absence of SUR1 in a luminescence-based surface-expression assay.
source: In a luminescence-based, surface-expression assay, we did not detect HA-tagged Kir6.2*-GFP at the plasma membrane in the absence of SUR1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the surface expression assay shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Both wild-type Kir6.2-GFP and Kir6.2*-GFP currents were inhibited to a similar extent by 100 µM tolbutamide when expressed with SUR1 (46.5% ±0.04% and 57.7% ±0.02%, respectively).
source: both wild-type Kir6.2-GFP and Kir6.2*-GFP currents were inhibited to a similar extent when expressed with SUR1 (46.5% ±0.04% and 57.7% ±0.02%, respectively; Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by patch-clamp data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Kir6.2*-GFP was co-assembled with SUR1 at the plasma membrane.
source: confirming that Kir6.2*-GFP was co-assembled with SUR1 at the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is inferred from the tolbutamide sensitivity data.

claim: Increasing the concentration of TNP-ATP caused a decrement in the ANAP peak at 472 nm and a concomitant increase in the TNP-ATP peak at 561 nm.
source: As expected from FRET, increasing the concentration of TNP-ATP caused a decrement in the ANAP peak at 472 nm and a concomitant increase in the TNP-ATP peak at 561 nm (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by spectroscopy data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The binding measurements were specific for the inhibitory nucleotide-binding site on Kir6.2.
source: We therefore conclude that our binding measurements were specific for the inhibitory nucleotide-binding site on Kir6.2.
evidence: This is inferred from the high Emax and the effect of the G334D mutation.

claim: The G334D mutation causes neonatal diabetes by preventing nucleotide binding.
source: This observation is consistent with the interpretation that the G334D mutation causes neonatal diabetes by preventing nucleotide binding.
evidence: This is inferred from the drastically reduced ANAP quenching in the G334D mutant.

claim: The apparent affinity of Kir6.2*-GFP + SUR1 for TNP-ATP in unroofed membranes was 25.6 µM.
source: The apparent affinity of Kir6.2*-GFP + SUR1 for TNP-ATP in unroofed membranes was 25.6 µM (Figure 1G and Table 1).
evidence: This is determined from Hill fits to the binding data shown in Figure 1G and Table 1.

claim: The apparent affinity for nucleotide inhibition measured using patch-clamp was 6.2 µM.
source: This value is higher than the apparent affinity for nucleotide inhibition (6.2 µM) measured using patch-clamp (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is determined from Hill fits to the current inhibition data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Current inhibition occurred at a lower range of concentrations compared to nucleotide binding.
source: Strikingly, current inhibition occurred at a lower range of concentrations compared to nucleotide binding (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the patch-clamp fluorometry data shown in Figure 2C,D.

claim: The MWC-type model fit the simultaneous binding and current measurements well.
source: Our simultaneous binding and current measurements were well fit with a Monod-Wyman-Changeux (MWC)-type model (Figure 2D,E; Monod et al., 1965)
evidence: This is demonstrated by the model fits shown in Figure 2D,E.

claim: C166 is located near the bundle-crossing gate of Kir6.2.
source: C166 is located near the bundle-crossing gate of Kir6.2 (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is based on structural data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Other mutations at the C166 site cause neonatal diabetes (Flanagan et al., 2006; Gloyn et al., 2006).
source: Other mutations at this site cause neonatal diabetes (Flanagan et al., 2006; Gloyn et al., 2006).
evidence: This is cited knowledge about disease-causing mutations.

claim: The C166S mutation suggests only a small change in apparent nucleotide affinity.
source: which suggests only a small change in apparent nucleotide affinity.
evidence: This is inferred from the similar EC50 values for Kir6.2*,C166S-GFP + SUR1 and Kir6.2*-GFP + SUR1.

claim: Whereas the apparent nucleotide binding affinity was unchanged by the C166S mutation, current inhibition occurred at much higher concentrations compared to binding and was incomplete.
source: Measuring current inhibition in combination with nucleotide binding confirmed that whereas the apparent nucleotide binding affinity was unchanged by the C166S mutation, current inhibition occurred at much higher concentrations compared to binding and was incomplete (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the patch-clamp fluorometry data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Only partial inhibition of Kir6.2*,C166S-GFP + SUR1 by 10 mM ATP was observed, which supports the existence of a nucleotide-insensitive current fraction at high concentrations.
source: However, we saw only partial inhibition of Kir6.2*,C166S-GFP + SUR1 by 10 mM ATP, which supports the existence of a nucleotide-insensitive current fraction at high concentrations.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the patch-clamp data.

claim: Partial inhibition at high nucleotide concentrations has been previously reported for mutations at Kir6.2-C166 in some constructs (Trapp et al., 1998; Ribalet et al., 2006) but not others (Enkvetchakul et al., 2001).
source: This observation has been previously reported for mutations at Kir6.2-C166 in some constructs (Trapp et al., 1998; Ribalet et al., 2006) but not others (Enkvetchakul et al., 2001).
evidence: This is cited knowledge about previous observations of C166 mutations.

claim: SUR1 increases the sensitivity of Kir6.2 to nucleotide inhibition (Babenko and Bryan, 2003; Chan, 2003; Fang et al., 2006).
source: However, it also increases the sensitivity of Kir6.2 to nucleotide inhibition (Babenko and Bryan, 2003; Chan, 2003; Fang et al., 2006).
evidence: This is cited knowledge about SUR1's effects on KATP.

claim: Kir6.2-GFP alone was much less sensitive to inhibition by TNP-ATP than Kir6.2-GFP + SUR1.
source: As expected Kir6.2-GFP alone was much less sensitive to inhibition by TNP-ATP than Kir6.2-GFP + SUR1.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the patch-clamp data.

claim: SUR1-K205 is located in the L0 linker of SUR1, which connects the first set of transmembrane domains (TMD0) to the ABC core structure (Figure 1A, Figure 4A; Martin et al., 2017; Puljung, 2018).
source: SUR1-K205 is located in the L0 linker of SUR1, which connects the first set of transmembrane domains (TMD0) to the ABC core structure (Figure 1A, Figure 4A; Martin et al., 2017; Puljung, 2018).
evidence: This is based on structural data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 4A.

claim: The L0 loop is adjacent to the inhibitory nucleotide-binding site on Kir6.2 and the interface between neighbouring Kir6.2 subunits.
source: This loop is adjacent to the inhibitory nucleotide-binding site on Kir6.2 and the interface between neighbouring Kir6.2 subunits.
evidence: This is based on structural data.

claim: Mutations at SUR1-K205 were previously shown to reduce sensitivity of KATP to nucleotide-dependent inhibition (Pratt et al., 2012; Ding et al., 2019).
source: Mutations at SUR1-K205 were previously shown to reduce sensitivity of KATP to nucleotide-dependent inhibition (Pratt et al., 2012; Ding et al., 2019)
evidence: This is cited knowledge about the effects of SUR1-K205 mutations.

claim: A recent cryo-EM structure suggests that SUR1-K205 may directly coordinate the phosphates of ATP bound to Kir6.2 (Ding et al., 2019).
source: and a recent cryo-EM stucture suggests that SUR1-K205 may directly coordinate the phosphates of ATP bound to Kir6.2 (Ding et al., 2019).
evidence: This is cited knowledge from a recent structural study.

claim: Other mutations in L0 are associated with neonatal diabetes (Ashcroft et al., 2017) and PHHI (Snider et al., 2013).
source: Other mutations in L0 are associated with neonatal diabetes (Ashcroft et al., 2017) and PHHI (Snider et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited knowledge about disease-causing mutations in L0.

claim: The binding and inhibition curves for TNP-ATP almost perfectly overlaid for the SUR1-K205A mutant.
source: The binding and inhibition curves for TNP-ATP almost perfectly overlaid for the SUR1-K205A mutant (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the patch-clamp fluorometry data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The binding and inhibition curves for TNP-ATP almost perfectly overlaid for the SUR1-K205E mutant.
source: The same was also true for SUR1-K205E (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the patch-clamp fluorometry data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Mutating K205 to an alanine or a glutamate resulted in an apparent decrease in nucleotide binding affinity.
source: Mutating K205 to an alanine or a glutamate resulted in an apparent decrease in nucleotide binding affinity (Figure 4C,D,E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the patch-clamp fluorometry data and model fits shown in Figure 4C,D,E.

claim: Mutating residue K205 reduced the ability of a single nucleotide to close the channel.
source: Whereas a single nucleotide-binding event is sufficient for channel closure when Kir6.2 is associated with wild-type SUR1, mutating residue K205 reduced the ability of a single nucleotide to close the channel.
evidence: This is inferred from the model fits and the shift in D.

claim: PCF allowed for site-specific measurement of nucleotide binding to KATP and concomitant measurements of channel current.
source: We have developed a novel approach that allows for site-specific measurement of nucleotide binding to KATP and concomitant measurements of channel current.
evidence: This is a summary of the methodological contribution of the study.

claim: Performing binding and current measurements simultaneously allowed examination of nucleotide regulation of KATP function in great detail.
source: Performing these measurements simultaneously allowed us to examine nucleotide regulation of KATP function in great detail.
evidence: This is a summary of the advantage of the PCF approach.

claim: Such insights would not be possible from experiments in which macroscopic currents or binding were measured in isolation.
source: Such insights would not be possible from experiments in which macroscopic currents or binding were measured in isolation.
evidence: This is a claim about the limitations of previous approaches.

claim: Saturating concentrations of MgTNP-ADP stabilized the open state by −1.9 kcal mol^-1 (−7.9 kJ mol^-1).
source: Based on our observations, saturating concentrations of MgTNP-ADP stabilied the open state by −1.9 kcal mol-1 (−7.9 kJ mol-1).
evidence: This is calculated from the E parameter derived from previous experiments.

claim: At saturating concentrations, TNP-ATP stabilized the closed state of KATP by −7.9 kcal mol^-1 (31.8 kJ mol^-1).
source: At saturating concentrations, TNP-ATP stabilied the closed state of KATP by −7.9 kcal mol-1 (31.8 kJ mol-1).
evidence: This is calculated from the D parameter derived from PCF experiments.

claim: Assuming excitatory and inhibitory processes are independent, inhibition would be expected to dominate under conditions at which all the nucleotide binding sites are occupied.
source: Thus, assuming excitatory and inhibitory processes are independent, inhibition would be expected to dominate under conditions at which all the nucleotide binding sites are occupied.
evidence: This is an inference from the calculated stabilization energies.

claim: This is consistent with published measurements of wild-type KATP in the presence of Mg2+ (Proks et al., 2010).
source: This is consistent with published measurements of wild-type KATP in the presence of Mg2+(Proks et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a comparison to cited knowledge.

claim: Higher affinity binding to the stimulatory site may explain the ability of MgADP to increase KATP currents in the presence of ATP (Gribble et al., 1998).
source: Higher affinity binding to the stimulatory site may explain the ability of MgADP to increase KATP currents in the presence of ATP (Gribble et al., 1998).
evidence: This is a speculation based on the KA values and cited knowledge.

claim: This phenomenon may also explain the bell-shaped MgADP concentration-response curve for KATP, which shows an increase in current at low concentrations, followed by inhibition at higher concentrations (Proks et al., 2010; Vedovato et al., 2015).
source: This phenomenon may also explain the bell-shaped MgADP concentration-response curve for KATP, which shows an increase in current at low concentrations, followed by inhibition at higher concentrations (Proks et al., 2010; Vedovato et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a speculation based on the KA values and cited knowledge.

claim: Mutations that cause neonatal diabetes reduce the sensitivity of KATP to nucleotide inhibition, and reduction in nucleotide sensitivity is broadly correlated with disease severity (McTaggart et al., 2010).
source: Mutations that cause neonatal diabetes reduce the sensitivity of KATP to nucleotide inhibition, and reduction in nucleotide sensitivity is broadly correlated with disease severity (McTaggart et al., 2010).
evidence: This is cited knowledge about neonatal diabetes mutations.

claim: This corroborates earlier hypotheses that mutating G334 directly disrupts inhibitory nucleotide binding to Kir6.2 (Drain et al., 1998).
source: This corroborates earlier hypotheses that mutating G334 directly disrupts inhibitory nucleotide binding to Kir6.2 (Drain et al., 1998).
evidence: This is a comparison to cited hypotheses.

claim: The C166S mutation does not directly affect nucleotide binding to Kir6.2, but rather disrupts the ability of bound nucleotide to close the channel.
source: In contrast to G334D, the C166S mutation does not directly affect nucleotide binding to Kir6.2, but rather disrupts the ability of bound nucleotide to close the channel.
evidence: This is inferred from the PCF data and model fits.

claim: In addition to directly contributing to tighter nucleotide binding at Kir6.2, SUR1 plays a critical role in preferentially stabilising the closed state of the channel when nucleotides are bound.
source: We find that, in addition to directly contributing to tighter nucleotide binding at Kir6.2, SUR1 plays a critical role in preferentially stabilising the closed state of the channel when nucleotides are bound.
evidence: This is inferred from the effects of SUR1-K205 mutations on both KA and D.

claim: Mutations in SUR1 that cause neonatal diabetes may do so by disrupting inhibitory binding/gating or enhancing the stimulatory effects of nucleotides.
source: Mutations in SUR1 that cause neonatal diabetes may do so by disrupting inhibitory binding/gating or enhancing the stimulatory effects of nucleotides.
evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanisms of disease-causing mutations.

claim: The formalism developed in this study provides a rigorous way to mechanistically assess the effects of these mutations.
source: The formalism developed in this study provides a rigorous way to mechanistically assess the effects of these mutations.
evidence: This is a claim about the utility of the study's approach.

claim: The PCF approach should be readily adaptable to the study of other nucleotide-gated channels including the cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR, also an ABC-family protein) and purinergic P2X receptors.
source: Our approach should be readily adaptable to the study of other nucleotide-gated channels including the cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR, also an ABC-family protein) and purinergic P2X receptors.
evidence: This is a speculation about the broader applicability of the method.
